opts: Most vascular region of bone (increased nutrition for organism)
Hair pin loop arrangement of blood vessels
questions.exp: Reasons: most vascular region (↑nutrition), hair pin loop arrangement → sluggish blood flow (easy exit to bone), few monocytes & macrophages (↓protection). (Book p138)

questions.q: Hair pin loop arrangement of metaphyseal blood vessels causes:
opts: Sluggish blood flow - easy exit of organism to bone
questions.exp: Hair pin loop arrangement → sluggish blood flow (easy exit to bone). (Book p138)

questions.q: In acute osteomyelitis, the organism reaches the metaphysis within:
questions.exp: Organism reaches metaphysis <24 hours → systemic manifestations: fever, pain. (Book p138)

questions.q: Systemic manifestations of acute osteomyelitis appear along with:
questions.exp: Organism reaches metaphysis <24 hours: systemic manifestations - fever, pain. (Book p138)

questions.q: Abscess in acute osteomyelitis is formed:
questions.exp: Abscess formed: after 24 hours. (Book p138)

questions.q: Sequestrum is:
opts: Dead bone formed inside the abscess

questions.q: Sinus in chronic osteomyelitis is:

questions.q: A young child with acute osteomyelitis presents with:
opts: High grade fever, pain & swelling, pseudoparalysis
Low grade fever with night sweats only
questions.exp: Young child: high grade fever, pain & swelling, pseudoparalysis. (Book p139)

questions.q: Pseudoparalysis in acute osteomyelitis means:
opts: Patient doesn't move the limb due to pain
questions.exp: Pseudoparalysis: patient doesn't move limb d/t pain. (Book p139)

questions.q: Causes of pseudoparalysis in a child include:
questions.exp: Causes of pseudoparalysis: septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, scurvy. (Book p139)

questions.q: In scurvy, pseudoparalysis occurs due to:
questions.exp: Scurvy (vit C deficiency): subperiosteal hemorrhage → pain → pseudoparalysis. (Book p139)

questions.q: Clinical hallmark of chronic osteomyelitis:
questions.exp: Chronic osteomyelitis: clinical hallmark is sinus. (Book p139)

questions.q: Pathological hallmark of acute osteomyelitis:
questions.exp: Acute: pathological hallmark abscess; chronic: sequestrum. (Book p139)

questions.q: Pathological hallmark of chronic osteomyelitis:
questions.exp: Chronic osteomyelitis: pathological hallmark sequestrum. (Book p139)

questions.q: Blood culture in acute osteomyelitis is positive in:
questions.exp: Blood culture: 50% +ve. (Book p139)

questions.q: WBC/neutrophil, ESR and CRP in acute osteomyelitis are:
questions.exp: WBC/neutrophil, ESR, CRP: high, not specific. (Book p139)

questions.q: Sensitive & specific blood marker for acute osteomyelitis and septic arthritis:
questions.exp: Serum procalcitonin: sensitive & specific marker for acute osteomyelitis and septic arthritis. (Book p139)

questions.q: Investigation that picks up the earliest changes (within 24 hrs of onset) in osteomyelitis:
questions.exp: MRI: picks up earliest changes within 24 hrs of disease onset - marrow edema. (Book p139)

questions.q: Isotopes used in bone scan for osteomyelitis:
questions.exp: Bone scan: technetium 99, gallium 67, indium 111 labelled WBC - accumulation in infection. (Book p139)

questions.q: X-ray changes in acute osteomyelitis are detected:
questions.exp: X-ray: changes detected after 24 hours of disease onset. (Book p139)

questions.q: Earliest X-ray change (within 48 hours) of acute osteomyelitis:
questions.exp: Earliest X-ray change (within 48 hours): soft tissue lucency/shadow around bone. (Book p139)

questions.q: Earliest bony change on X-ray (7-10 days/2 weeks) in osteomyelitis:
questions.exp: Earliest bony changes on X-ray (7-10 days/2 weeks): periosteal reaction. (Book p139)

questions.q: Gold standard investigation of osteomyelitis:
opts: Biopsy - tissue sample from site of infection
questions.exp: Biopsy: gold standard; tissue sample collected from site of infection. (Book p140)

questions.q: Definitive treatment of acute osteomyelitis presenting within 24 hours:
questions.exp: Presents within 24 hours: antibiotics ± drain the abscess. (Book p140)

questions.q: Definitive treatment of acute osteomyelitis presenting after 24 hours:
questions.exp: Presents after 24 hours: antibiotics + drain the abscess. (Book p140)

questions.q: Supportive treatment of acute osteomyelitis includes:
opts: Initial broad spectrum antibiotics, analgesics, antipyretics, rest & splint, icepack & elevation
questions.exp: Supportive: initial broad spectrum antibiotics, analgesics (pain), antipyretics (fever), rest & splint to prevent movement (↓pain), icepack & limb elevation (swelling). (Book p140)

questions.q: Total antibiotic duration in acute osteomyelitis:
opts: 6 weeks - 2 weeks IV followed by 4 weeks PO
questions.exp: 6 weeks: 2 weeks IV → 4 weeks PO. (Book p140)

questions.q: Long antibiotic duration in osteomyelitis is required due to:
opts: Low penetration of drug in bone

questions.q: Response to antibiotic therapy in osteomyelitis is assessed using:
questions.exp: Response assessed using CRP measurements. (Book p140)

questions.q: Most common complication of acute osteomyelitis:
questions.exp: Complications: chronic osteomyelitis (m/c). (Book p140)

questions.q: Spread of acute osteomyelitis to joint (septic arthritis) is prevented by:
questions.exp: Septic arthritis: bone → joint; prevented by growth plate. (Book p140)

opts: <1 year - before growth plate formation; adults after growth plate fusion
questions.exp: Common in: <1 yr (before growth plate formation) and adults (after growth plate fusion). (Book p140)

questions.q: Other complications of acute osteomyelitis besides chronic osteomyelitis and septic arthritis:
questions.exp: Complications: chronic OM (m/c), septic arthritis, septicemia, growth disturbance. (Book p140)

questions.q: Subacute osteomyelitis lasts:

questions.q: Chronic osteomyelitis is defined as infection lasting:

opts: Dead, dense, devascularized bone inside abscess
questions.exp: Sequestrum: pathological hallmark of chronic osteomyelitis - dead, dense, devascularized bone inside abscess. (Book p141)

questions.q: Annular/ring sequestrum is seen at:

questions.q: Feathery/flake/coarse sandy sequestrum is seen in:

questions.q: Button hole sequestrum occurs:

questions.q: Ivory sequestrum is classically associated with:

questions.q: X-ray in chronic osteomyelitis shows:

units.title: Infections: Site & Etiology
units.guide: Bone plus medullary cavity is osteomyelitis (metaphysis of long bone); joint is septic arthritis. Bacteria rule - pyogenes burn with severe periosteal reaction while TB smoulders with a limited one, except in the short bones of hand and foot where even TB flares.

units.title: Routes of Infection
units.guide: Children and the elderly fall first - low immunity. The bloodstream seeds bone from a pre-existing focus most often; puncture wounds, surgery and open fractures inoculate directly, and a septic joint can chew its way into bone.

units.title: Staph aureus
units.guide: Staphylococcus aureus is king of musculoskeletal infection - the m/c cause of osteomyelitis overall, acute and chronic, in rich and poor countries alike, in HIV, open fractures and post-surgery.

units.title: Special-Case Organisms
units.guide: Memorise the pairing grid: sickle cell - Salmonella diaphyseal (metaphysis means Staph); IV drugs - Pseudomonas; animal bite - Pasteurella; human bite - Eikenella; long parenteral lines - fungi.

units.title: Site & Metaphyseal Preference
units.guide: Children break their femur distally then tibia; adults guard their vertebrae. The metaphysis beckons organisms: most vascular soil, hair-pin vessels with sluggish flow, and few patrolling macrophages.

units.title: Acute OM: Pathophysiology Timeline
units.guide: The clock: organism lands in metaphysis <24 h with fever and pain; after 24 h an abscess pools; dead bone (sequestrum) drops inside it; periosteum builds the involucrum by about 10 days; a break in involucrum is cloaca, in skin a sinus - pus escapes.

units.title: Clinical Features
units.guide: A young child with high fever, painful swollen limb that he refuses to move - pseudoparalysis. Think septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, or scurvy's subperiosteal bleed.

units.title: Acute vs Chronic Hallmarks
units.guide: Two-by-two: acute has fever-and-pain clinically and an abscess pathologically; chronic announces a sinus and hides a sequestrum.

units.title: Blood Investigations
units.guide: Blood culture catches the bug half the time; WBC, ESR, CRP rise but accuse no one; serum procalcitonin alone is both sensitive and specific for acute osteomyelitis and septic arthritis.

units.title: Radiology Timeline
units.guide: MRI sees marrow edema within 24 h; bone scan glows with Tc99, Ga67, In111-WBC; X-ray waits a day, shows soft tissue shadow by 48 h, and only at 7-10 days lifts the periosteal veil.

units.title: Biopsy & Treatment
units.guide: Biopsy from the site is gold standard. Within 24 h antibiotics may suffice, after 24 h add drainage; six weeks of antibiotics (2 IV, 4 oral) because bone drinks drugs poorly - track the fall of CRP, and splint, cool and elevate meanwhile.

units.title: Complications of Acute OM
units.guide: Chronicity tops the list; pus may cross to the joint where the growth plate is missing - under 1 year or after fusion - and septicemia and growth disturbance complete the four.

units.title: Durations & Chronic OM
units.guide: Cut the timeline at 2 and 4 weeks: acute under two, subacute two-to-four, chronic beyond four - chronic is simply acute osteomyelitis that never died, wearing a sinus as its badge.

units.title: Sequestrum
units.guide: A dead, dense, devascularized island of bone floating in pus, wrapped in granulation tissue and involucrum, its haversian systems destroyed - the pathological signature of chronicity.

units.title: Types of Sequestrum
units.guide: Shape names the disease: coral for Perthe's, ring for pins and stumps, tubular for pyogenic infection, feathery sandy for TB, fine sandy for viral, button-hole after radiation, ivory for syphilis.

units.title: Chronic OM: Workup & Initial Rx
units.guide: X-ray unmasks sequestrum, involucrum and cloaca; dye through the sinus maps its track; biopsy remains gold standard - start broad-spectrum antibiotics and support the patient.

units.title: Surgery for Chronic OM
units.guide: The operative ladder under antibiotic cover: sequestrectomy, curettage to the Paprika blush, saucerization, dead space filled with graft or cement, skin flapped or VAC'd at -75 to -125 mmHg - never on eschar or tumor.

units.title: Chronic OM Complications
units.guide: Pathological fracture comes first, sinuses can turn squamous, and flare-ups and amyloidosis round out the toll of a chronic discharging wound.

units.title: Variants & Brodie's Abscess
units.guide: Strong host, weak bug - infection walled off without sinus or sequestrum. Brodie's: subacute, proximal tibia, pus positive, dull ache with low fever, a lucent eye ringed by sclerotic rim - penumbra on MRI - treat with antibiotics ± debridement.

units.title: Garre's Sclerosing OM
units.guide: Garré's: the dry chronic twin - mandible more than tibia, no pus, no raised ESR, just bony hard swelling and bone gone rock-dense from excessive periosteal reaction; antibiotics suffice.

units.title: Septic Arthritis: Basics
units.guide: Pus in a joint is a surgical emergency - undrained it digests cartilage. Under-five children and the elderly, blood-borne Staph aureus (Pseudomonas in addicts, gonococcus in the sexually active), knee first, hip in infants - Tom Smith.

units.title: Septic Arthritis: Clinical
units.guide: Swollen, red, exquisitely painful joint held still; the limb rests where the capsule is slackest - hip in FABER, knee at 5-30 degrees - and the knee offers a positive patellar tap.

units.title: Septic Arthritis: Investigations
units.guide: Bloods and culture, an early film that shows little but a widened space, late destruction, MRI synovial thickening - and ultrasound-guided arthrocentesis that both names the culprit and relieves the joint.

units.title: Rx & Ankylosis Types
units.guide: Arthrotomy with irrigation and debridement is TOC; neglect lets collagenases strip cartilage until raw bones fuse - bony ankylosis. Disease fusion is ankylosis (bony from pyogenic/TB spine - stable, painless; fibrous from TB - mobile, painful, unstable), surgery's is arthrodesis.

units.title: Tom Smith Arthritis
units.guide: Infant's septic hip under one year: pus and enzymes dissolve the cartilaginous capital epiphysis - chondrolysis - leaving a hypermobile, shortened limb with positive telescopy.

units.title: Transient Synovitis & Kocher's
units.guide: A post-viral, self-limiting 'observation hip' of 6-12 year olds: limp, mild fever, position of ease. Joint aspiration is the best divider, Kocher counts four points - weight bearing, >38.5°C, ESR >40, WBC >12,000 - the more, the more septic. Limp in a child: transient synovitis first.

units.title: Paronychia
units.guide: The commonest hand infection runs around the nail - Staph aureus again; drain it, and if it sneaks under the nail bed, lift a piece of nail.

units.title: Felon (Whitlow)
units.guide: Pulp-space abscess of the distal phalanx, thumb first: a tense throbbing digit that can erode into bone or tendon; a vertical incision breaks the septae and lets the pus go.

units.title: Tenosynovitis
units.guide: Infected tendon sheath: finger held flexed, fusiform swelling, pain on passive extension and Kanavel's tap - antibiotics plus incision and drainage.
